title: Can the detection probability be formalized

problemStatement.formal: For d >= 2 and a base b with b % d = 1, count the residues detected by the digit-sum perturbation test and prove the detected proportion is (d - 1) / d in cardinal form.
problemStatement.plain: Formalizes how often digit-sum divisibility checks detect perturbations: among residues modulo d, exactly d - 1 nonzero residues are detected and one zero residue is undetected.
whyMatters: Detection-rate claims make divisibility tests quantitative instead of only yes/no rules.
Counting the detected and undetected residue classes explains why mod 9 catches eight out of nine nonzero decimal digit-sum errors.
The same residue-counting argument applies to decimal, octal, hexadecimal, and arbitrary bases satisfying b == 1 mod d.

proven: Powers of the base remain 1 modulo d when b % d = 1 (Lean: base_pow_mod_one).
Digit perturbations preserve the expected modular behavior (Lean: perturbation_mod, dvd_mul_pow_iff, digit_sum_perturbation).
The file counts multiples and nonmultiples in the residue interval 1..d (Lean: unique_multiple_in_range, multiples_in_range, undetected_count, detected_count).
The detection-rate identity is proved in cardinal form: detected_count * d = (d - 1) * d (Lean: detection_rate_ratio).
Concrete decimal, octal, hexadecimal, and trivial binary cases are verified, including nines_better_than_threes.
knownResults.goal: Document the verified residue-counting proof for digit-sum detection rates and its concrete base examples.
